articles.body: Dennis Quaid is shedding light on what his day-to-day life in Nashville looks like six years after leaving Los Angeles behind. "Basically, I play golf," the actor told People. "I love to be around the house here. You get a lot of land and space, but you’re still in an urban environment. I’ve made some really good friends here to spend time with. It’s important and a great place to raise a family." Quaid and his wife, Laura Savoie, moved to Tennessee in 2020 after living in California for decades. Quaid told the outlet that the connection to the community he found in Nashville makes it feel like home. He also told the outlet that the entertainment industry in Hollywood has drastically changed since his early days as an actor. You met a lot of people that way and that’s where a community was formed," Quaid told the outlet. "It’s important and a great place to raise a family." He explained that the system has changed and actors are now largely sending in self-taped auditions, which has left him yearning for the sense of community he once felt. articles.title: Harano Sur: Uttam Kumar at 100
articles.summary: At a hundred, Uttam Kumar, the Mahanayak or great hero of Bengali cinema, is the most agreed-upon man in Bengal. The agreement conceals a long negotia.
articles.body: At a hundred, Uttam Kumar, the Mahanayak or great hero of Bengali cinema, is the most agreed-upon man in Bengal. The agreement conceals a long negotiation, in which Bengal accepted certain things about him, refused others outright, and has still not accepted the one obligation that matters.The centenary arrived on schedule on September 3 and with better than usual paraphernalia: statues garlanded at Tollygunge, the home of the Bengali film industry, and at Ahiritola, the north Kolkata street where he was born; a twenty-foot cutout outside the iconic single-screen Bijoli cinema; a padayatra with artistes; LED vans doing the rounds; an exhibition of booklets and behind-the-scenes stills at Nandan, the state-run film centre; and a commemorative stamp and cover from the Department of Posts.And, beyond the day itself, the apparatus of a year: a foundation stone in New Town for a film centre on three acres; a twenty-member advisory board with the Chief Minister as chief patron; a year-long calendar; and a festival opening, inevitably, with Nayak, Satyajit Ray's study of a matinee idol, written for him.The Prime Minister posted a tribute in the morning and directed everyone to what he had said about the actor on Mann Ki Baat, his monthly radio address, the previous Sunday: that he had kept working through early failure, and should be admired for it. All of this is true, and almost none of it is interesting, because perseverance is the one quality you can commemorate without showing anybody a film.The more useful question on a hundredth birth anniversary is not what Bengal loved about Uttam Kumar. Bengal has been answering that compulsively since July 1980, when he died. The more interesting question is what Bengal was prepared to accept from him, and what it was not.From Flop Master General to MahanayakBegin with the acceptance, because it was neither instant nor free.Arun Kumar Chattopadhyay was born on 3 September 1926 at his maternal home on Ahiritola Street, in north Kolkata, the son of a man who ran the projector at the Metro cinema, which is to say that he came to the cinema through the back of the hall.He matriculated in the second division, took a clerk's job at the Port Commissioners on two hundred and seventy-five rupees a month, changed his screen name three times before one finally stuck, and by twenty-six had accumulated enough failure for the trade to nickname him the Flop Master General, a joke reportedly performed to his face on studio floors. Then came Nirmal Dey's Basu Paribar in 1952 and Sharey Chuattor in 1953, then Agni Pariksha in 1954, and a Bengal that had laughed at him for four years decided, within two, that he was the only face it wanted to look at.What it had decided to look at was itself, improved.The Bengali Uttam Kumar played was urban, salaried, educated, courteous and emotionally contained, a man who could be poor without being coarse and prosperous without becoming a boor, and he arrived exactly when a post-Partition middle class, remade by the 1947 division of Bengal and the refugees it drove west, needed evidence that such a man could still exist in Calcutta.The Encyclopaedia of Indian Cinema puts it more precisely than most tributes will this week, noting that his early romances revived the humanist tradition of the bhadralok, Bengal's respectable, educated middle class, while quietly discarding some of its more conservative furniture. He was a lover who did not chase; he waited, in Saptapadi, and returned much later to the wreckage, in Jatugriha. He made room for his heroines instead of rescuing them. Bengal accepted him because he flattered it in a register it recognised as good taste, which is the only kind of flattery the bhadralok has ever accepted.Three things Bengal withheldHaving granted him that, it began withholding other things.First, the ordinary latitude it might have extended to a private citizen. In 1963 he left the house he shared with Gauri Devi, whom he had married in 1948 and never divorced, and lived for the next seventeen years with the actress Supriya Devi. The audience that had built a cult around his on-screen restraint then conducted a running commentary on the arrangement for the rest of his life and a good while after it. Bengal was happy to watch him play a murderer in Kuhak, a rotting landlord in Stree, a bought politician in Bagh Bondi Khela. What it would not do was allow the man anything the character might have got away with.Second, it withheld the national career.He turned down Bees Saal Baad, turned down the second lead in Sangam, and then, in 1967, produced his own Hindi debut, Chhoti Si Mulaqat, a remake of Agni Pariksha with Vyjayanthimala in place of Suchitra Sen, his partner in the original and the other half of Bengali cinema's definitive screen couple. It failed so spectacularly that it left him close to bankruptcy. Bombay took him properly only once, with Shakti Samanta's Amanush in 1975, shot in Bengali and Hindi at the same time, which ran for the better part of two years and became the biggest hit of his career; when the same team tried again with Ananda Ashram, the Bengali version ran for months and the Hindi one died.There is no evidence that Bengal mourned any of this. A Mahanayak who belonged equally to Bombay would have stopped being quite so completely Bengal's property, and one of the uses of Uttam Kumar was precisely that he proved Bengal did not need Bombay's permission to produce a star.Third, and most instructively, Bengal withheld the right to be anybody else.On 23 September 1976, All India Radio dropped Birendra Krishna Bhadra's Mahishasuramardini, the recital that had woken Bengal before dawn every Mahalaya since the 1930s, on the day that opens the Durga Puja season. In its place came a new programme narrated by Uttam Kumar and scored by Hemanta Mukherjee, known outside Bengal as Hemant Kumar, which is to say by the two most beloved voices in the province. Listeners stoned Akashvani Bhavan, All India Radio's Kolkata headquarters. The switchboard was overwhelmed, demonstrations were held in Calcutta and elsewhere, the ministry was forced to climb down, Bhadra was restored, and the new version was exiled to Sashthi, the sixth day of the Puja, where it has survived ever since as a curiosity. It took Bengal roughly a fortnight to reject the most popular man it had ever produced, on the one occasion he stepped outside the frame it had built for him. He apologised. He did not try again.Worshipped, but not readThe most consequential withholding, however, came from his own constituency's clerisy.Bengal in his lifetime had a critical establishment that treated popular cinema as an embarrassment to be tolerated in the interests of the box office. The result was that the first actor in India to win the National Award for Best Actor, given to him in 1968, the first year of the category, for Antony Firingee and Ray's Chiriyakhana, generated a myth and remarkably little scholarship. Sayandeb Chowdhury, whose 2021 book remains the only serious critical biography, describes a star kept in a kind of solitary confinement by his own fame, and notes how little Bengal's learned circles bothered to understand his range, his production work or his stewardship of an entire industry.Ray, who wrote Nayak for him and about him, had no such difficulty and said plainly that there would not be another like him. It is a peculiar arrangement in which the director is canonised, the star is worshipped, and only one of them gets read.The industry's balance sheetThat stewardship is the part of the legend the garlands rarely reach.Uttam Kumar produced films from 1957, directed from 1966, composed music for Kal Tumi Aleya, and in 1968 left the existing actors' body to set up Shilpi Sangshad, a welfare organisation for technicians and small artistes, running it until his death. When the fund ran dry, he made a film to replenish it: Bon Palashir Padabali in 1973, which he directed himself while persuading some of the industry's biggest names to work for nothing. It went on to become the year's highest earner.He was not merely the ornament of Bengali cinema. For thirty years he was, to an extraordinary extent, its balance sheet, which is why the industry did not simply mourn him in 1980 but visibly began to falter without him, and why Anandabazar Patrika, Bengal's largest Bengali daily, could compress the event into two words: Cholochitre Indrapatan, the fall of Indra in the cinema, which is Bengali for the toppling of a colossus.Why governments prefer birthdaysWhich brings us to the present negotiation, and to what is being accepted this week.For four decades, remembering Uttam Kumar was centred on 24 July, the anniversary of his death, and took place largely in a folk register: Shilpi Sangshad's own festival at Nandan, the retrospectives, the television reruns, the Mahanayak Samman that the previous government instituted in 2012 and handed out every July at Uttam Mancha, the south Kolkata auditorium named after him. The centenary completes a migration that has been under way for some years, from the day he died to the day he was born, which is to say from a mourning that belonged to the audience to an anniversary that can belong to the state.Governments prefer birthdays. Birthdays are about arrival.Every government has taken its turn. The Left Front, then in power in West Bengal, put up the Tollygunge statue in 1993. The metro station was renamed and the first stamp issued in 2009. The Trinamool Congress government created the award in 2012. A BJP government four months old in Bengal, looking for a Bengali inheritance nobody can reasonably contest, has now given him a year, a board, a stamp, three acres and a padayatra, with the Prime Minister supplying the moral.Nobody in this sequence needs to be insincere, which is precisely the difficulty. Uttam Kumar is loved almost without exception, and a figure loved without exception is available to everybody. Standing next to that smile has never cost a politician a single vote.The vaults nobody has openedWhat none of them has accepted is custody.In 2018, when the Film Heritage Foundation brought its restoration workshop to the Kolkata International Film Festival, its founder, the archivist and filmmaker Shivendra Singh Dungarpur, pointed out that Bengal had lost every silent film it made between 1918 and the early thirties and that his foundation had identified more than a hundred Bengali titles in need of urgent rescue. On that list sits Harano Sur, the 1957 film Uttam Kumar produced himself, the year's biggest earner, whose title translates as the lost tune.Soumitra Chatterjee, Ray's other great leading man and the only serious rival Uttam Kumar had for the Bengali audience, was asked about the same crisis and said he doubted whether the classics of Barua, the Devdas director P.C. Barua, or Uttam Kumar, or even his own early work, could still be saved. Eight years later, the state's own information secretary describes Uttam Mancha as dilapidated, the film directorate's brief already includes restoration of the holdings in government vaults, and yet the most basic public question remains unanswered: which of Uttam Kumar's two hundred and eleven films survive as negatives, which survive as scratched prints, which exist only in some distributor's family cupboard, and which are simply gone?Meanwhile, the state says the purpose of all this is to introduce him to a generation that missed him.That generation's actual access too often consists of YouTube uploads mastered from video cassettes, and Oti Uttam, the Bengali director Srijit Mukherji's 2024 film in which the Mahanayak appears as a ghost assembled from footage drawn from fifty-four of his own films, with his voice cloned by an American AI company because there was no other way left to make him speak a new line. The exercise cost about a crore and a half.Sit with that for a moment: a generation that has rarely had the chance to see a clean print of Chowringhee has already paid to watch a synthetic reconstruction of the man who was in it.The appetite is proven. The supply is a policy failure.The test is 2036So let the padayatra proceed, and let the foundation stone be laid. The test of this centenary will not be what gets unveiled between now and next September, but whether, in 2036, a nineteen-year-old in Barrackpore can watch a properly restored Jatugriha on a legal platform, in a decent transfer, subtitled by somebody who knows Bengali.Publish the vault inventory. Fund restoration before construction. Clear the rights, which are scattered across heirs and defunct distributors and grow harder to trace every year.Bengal has spent a century deciding what it would and would not accept from Uttam Kumar. The one thing he actually needs from us now is the one obligation we have still not accepted.The lost tune (harano sur) stays lost, cutout notwithstanding.Give your child the gift of confidence! articles.title: El llamativo momento entre Máximo Huerta, Iván Redondo y Cristina Pardo en ‘La Mesa’: “Mal rollo”
articles.standfirst: Antena 3 estrenó este nuevo programa con la expresentadora de ‘Más Vale Tarde’ al frente
articles.summary: Antena 3 estrenó este nuevo programa con la expresentadora de ‘Más Vale Tarde’ al frente
articles.body: Antena 3 estrenó este miércoles, 2 de septiembre, ‘La Mesa’, un nuevo programa para esta temporada de la mano de Cristina Pardo y lo hizo con colaboradores de alto calado como Iván Redondo y Máximo Huerta. Pues bien, entre ellos tres se vivió un momento curioso, ya que Huerta le pidió a la presentadora cambiarse de silla tras haber sido usada por Iván Redondo. En primera instancia, apareció Redondo, quien se pronunció acerca de la gestión que está haciendo el Gobierno y su equipo con lo que pasa en Ceuta, algo en lo que Huerta también opinó en la misma dirección. No obstante, el escritor, una vez sentado en la otra silla del plató, dijo lo siguiente a Cristina Pardo, instándole a cambiar el mueble: “Me quiero cambiar de silla. En la silla de Iván Redondo, no. La de Iván Redondo, no. Me lo vas a permitir. Esto me va a dar mala suerte". Cabe recordar que Huerta coincidió con Redondo en el Gobierno cuando fue nombrado ministro de Cultura y Deporte, algo en lo que tan solo estuvo siete días, ya que se dio a conocer que esquivó un pago de más de 200.00 euros a Hacienda. Esto causó la respuesta de la presentadora del nuevo programa de Antena 3: “Tú coincidiste con Iván Redondo en el Gobierno cuando él era jefe de gabinete, ¿no?". A ello respondió Máximo Huerta de manera afirmativa: "En uno de los momentos más fuertes de mi vida y al sentarme me ha dado un mal rollo... y por eso te lo he pedido así, que como no hay falso directo ni nada". “Pero, ¿qué pasa? ¿Él participó en tu salida del Gobierno?", apostilló la televisiva, a lo que el de Utiel respondió: "Uno de los peores días de mi vida es Iván Redondo y yo conectando con Alsina. Con lo cual digo 'joder, qué noche, querida”. "Entonces es como tener un déjà vu horroroso", sentenció Cristina Pardo al respecto, antes de presentar a la siguiente colaboradora, que será Ivana Rodríguez, la hermana de Georgina Rodriguez

She asked Paul if she ever thought Mason “looks like Dakota,” in reference to Paul’s ex-boyfriend, Dakota Mortensen, with whom Paul shares a son. “I didn’t start thinking that until people said it around me,” Paul said. “They have the same initials,” Draper responded. “They’re both from Idaho. It’s so weird.” Paul then left her “Mormon Wives” castmates stunned when she revealed how her experience filming “The Bachelorette” ended. “And yes, he did get down on one knee and proposed, which I was shocked,” she said. Paul said she accepted the proposal. “And then I come home,” she said. She said she returned to Utah and began texting Mortensen. “I don’t know how it led to it, but he came over,” Paul said. Paul’s season of “The Bachelorette” was canceled in March after TMZ published a video reportedly from an altercation between Paul and Mortensen in 2023 that led to her arrest. Paul later pled guilty in abeyance to aggravated assault, court records obtained by NBC News show. The former couple was also involved in a domestic violence investigation earlier this year stemming from several alleged incidents from 2024 to 2026, police confirmed to NBC News. Reps for Mortensen and Paul declined to comment at the time. In April, the Salt Lake County District Attorney’s Office said neither Paul nor Mortensen would face new charges. Filming for Season 5 of “Mormon Wives” was paused amid the investigation but picked back up around late April. “Secret Lives of Mormon Wives” will return for Season 5 on Sept. 10.

articles.title: LISA Says BLACKPINK Has to ‘Hide When We’re Dating’ & Recalls Having Secret Relationships
articles.summary: "I didn’t want my dating to be the thing that hurts BLACKPINK's popularity," the star explains in her new documentary.
articles.body:
BLACKPINK 's members have stayed private about their love lives for as long as they've been making music, and in her new documentary, LISA explained why.

At one point in Always Lalisa — which is set to premiere soon at the Toronto International Film Festival — the Thai performer opened up about the restrictions K-pop culture places on idols when it comes to romance. "In K-pop culture, we can't date," she said, according to a report by Toronto Star published Thursday (Sept. 3). "If you're seeing someone and you get caught by paparazzi, your popularity drops."

"When I was younger, I had a few relationships, but we had to hide when we're dating," she continued. "I didn't want my dating to be the thing that hurts BLACKPINK's popularity."

She also revealed in the film that her song "Dream," which appears on her Billboard 200 top 10 solo album Alter Ego , is about one of her past secret relationships. LISA added that she got that person's blessing before releasing the song, so long as fans wouldn't be able to uncover who'd inspired it.

"They thought they figured it out, but I don't think so," LISA said.

The Sue Kim-directed documentary will screen on Sept. 11 at TIFF, after which it'll hit theaters in October and later stream exclusively on YouTube Premium. According to a description, it follows the White Lotus actress' "transformative year away from BLACKPINK" as "forging her own path, particularly in the Western music market, brings new pressures, relentless scrutiny and the challenge of redefining herself on her own terms."

LISA is now gearing up to release her first set of solo songs since Alter Ego , with EP Press Play set to drop on Oct. 23. Its first single, "SaWaDiKa," arrived Friday (Sept. 4).

articles.title: Steve Irwin’s Cameraman Details His Final Moments With Stingray Amid 20th Anniversary of His Death
articles.summary: Steve Irwin‘s cameraman, Justin Lyons, recently recalled the tragic moment a stingray fatally pierced the chest of the late conservationist while they were f...
articles.body:
Steve Irwin's cameraman, Justin Lyons, recounted the tragic moment when a stingray fatally pierced the late conservationist's chest while filming a documentary at the Great Barrier Reef.

Lyons shared that they had filmed with stingrays many times before, but the final shot went awry when the stingray mistook Irwin for a tiger shark and started stabbing towards him with its tail.

Despite efforts to save him, Steve Irwin fell unconscious and passed away at age 44 after being pierced in the chest by the stingray, leaving his family and crew devastated.

Steve Irwin 's cameraman, Justin Lyons , recently recalled the tragic moment a stingray fatally pierced the chest of the late conservationist while they were filming a documentary at the Great Barrier Reef.

Lyons participated in a 60 Minutes Australia documentary titled Steve Irwin: A Wild Life , which aired on Wednesday, September 2, to mark 20 years since the man dubbed "The Crocodile Hunter" died.

In the documentary, Lyons shared that filming with stingrays was nothing new for the two men, as they'd done it "a hundred times before."

Before things took a turn for the worse on September 4, 2006, Lyons said he got multiple shots of the TV personality with a "massive" bull ray stingray. They then wanted to get the "final shot, which would be the opening shot, because "by now the stingray was calm," he said. However, it did not go as planned.

"The stingray is in front of me, buried in the sand. He swims up, swims over the top of it. It doesn't move. But as he's directly over the top of it, of course, it thought he was a tiger shark and started stabbing madly towards him with its tail," Lyons recounted. "The water just boiled. I couldn't see anything that was going on. Bubbles and thrashing and then all of a sudden it stopped, and the stingray swam away. The water calmed. So I just panned with the stingray … I let it go out of shot as I panned back to Steve. He came jumping up out of the water, screaming, and the water around him was now full of blood."

"He screamed out, 'It's punctured me lung.' I threw the camera into one of the rubber duckies, drag Steve into the boat," Lyons remembered. "His khaki shirt is open, and he's just got blood pouring out of a gash like that in his chest right over his heart. But he's conscious, and he says to me, looks me right in the eye, and he says, 'I'm dying.'"

The father of two — who shares Bindi , 28, and Robert , 22, with wife Terri — then fell unconscious as they went back to his boat, Croc One, where the crew attempted CPR on him for 45 minutes while they raced to Low Island.

"I just remember us putting in a massive effort to get him up the beach, put him in a little hut, and then I heard a chopper landing, and that was paramedics arriving, and I had this absolute sense of relief. I was like, 'Oh my god, they'll be able to bring him back to life. They will save him,'" Lyons said. "But within about 10 seconds of them being there, they just said, 'No, he's gone.' And then it really hit me. It was like absolute despair."

Over the years since his death at age 44, Terri, 62, Bindi, and Robert have honored Steve through their work at Australia Zoo.

articles.title: Rabbinic group accuses Jewish entertainers of 'whitewashing antisemitism' in Mark Ruffalo defense
articles.summary: The Coalition for Jewish Values accused over 170 Jewish entertainers of whitewashing antisemitism by defending Mark Ruffalo's merger criticism.
articles.body: FIRST ON FOX — A rabbinic group is calling out some Jewish entertainers for "whitewashing antisemitism" by supporting actor Mark Ruffalo after his harsh opposition to the proposed Warner Bros. Discovery-Paramount merger. More than 170 Jewish entertainers and artists signed a letter Tuesday "proudly" voicing support for Ruffalo after he was accused of antisemitism when criticizing the proposed $111 billion merger. Coalition for Jewish Values, which represents over 2,500 traditional, Orthodox rabbis in American public policy, said it typically does not respond when a Hollywood figure says something it finds hateful about Jews or Israel. But the group believes Ruffalo’s comments forced a group of Jewish Hollywood figures that have "little knowledge of Jewish history or the nature of antisemitism" to "deny obvious bigotry." MORE THAN 180 JEWISH ENTERTAINERS RALLY BEHIND ACTOR MARK RUFFALO IN PROTEST LETTER "Ruffalo did not merely criticize a business deal. In an August 22 Instagram post tying the Paramount-Skydance/Warner Bros. merger to Oracle's work with Israel, Ruffalo claimed that the Ellison family — who are Jewish — were ‘powering some of the most destructive and inhuman forces in the world,’ and framed a corporate transaction as built on ‘genocide’ and ‘apartheid.’ That is not policy criticism, but mischaracterization of civil rights for Jews and Arabs as racism, and the rescue of Jewish hostages as murder," the Coalition for Jewish Values said in a statement. "Nonetheless, more than 170 Jewish entertainment figures rushed to sign a letter dismissing the antisemitism charge as an ‘outrageous smear campaign.’ To be certain, they are entitled to their ignorant and misguided views," the statement continued. "They are not, however, entitled to be taken seriously when they engage in whitewashing antisemitism, or suggest that those with sufficient discernment to recognize the oldest of anti-Jewish tropes should deny the obvious." The group said that "America set itself apart from much of the world precisely by declaring hatred of Jews unwelcome, regardless of who dressed it up as righteousness," and feels "Ruffalo would do well to remember that he owes much of his career to the Founding Fathers who made America so hospitable, and the Jews who fled persecution in Europe to build new homes for their children in a friendlier land." JOHN CUSACK STANDS IN 'SOLIDARITY' WITH MARK RUFFALO AMID PARAMOUNT'S ANTISEMITISM ALLEGATION "It is some of those children, working in New York in the early 20th century, who created Marvel Comics and invented The Incredible Hulk," the group said. Rabbi Yaakov Menken, executive vice president of the Coalition for Jewish Values, told Fox News Digital that Ruffalo's remarks were "embarrassing" and that Ruffalo presented a "mythical inversion" of the situation in the Middle East. Ruffalo was accused of invoking "antisemitic tropes" by Paramount after the Marvel star shared a video from August of Safra Catz, an Oracle executive vice chair and Paramount board member, discussing technology Oracle used to assist Israel after the Oct. 7 Hamas terrorist attack. He linked Oracle co-founder Larry Ellison, the father of Paramount CEO David Ellison, to financing behind the proposed acquisition and suggested the merger would be used to push "oppression." "These ‘really profoundly scary technologies’ will most likely be merged into one of the largest media conglomerates in the world and one day used on you," Ruffalo said. "Look how she revels in what we now have come to see as a genocide, which was built on an apartheid system of oppression powered by Oracle." ANTISEMITIC VIOLENCE REACHES DEADLIEST LEVEL SINCE 1994, NEW GLOBAL REPORT FINDS Among the Jewish artists who signed the letter were Abbi Jacobson, Alex Winter, Gina Gershon, Ilana Glazer, James Schamus, Joel Coen, Larry Charles, Kate Berlant, Naomi Klein, Sarah Sherman, Jane Schoenbrun, Todd Haynes and Tony Kushner, denied Ruffalo‘s comments were antisemitic, arguing that the executives Ruffalo criticized had "themselves have explicitly linked to their support for the ongoing depredations being visited on the people of Palestine and their silencing of critics of those horrors." The celebrities also argued that a majority of American Jews now believe that Israel committed war crimes against Gaza, with a significant portion believing Israel is guilty of genocide. They called for an end to "spurious charges of antisemitism" against people like Ruffalo. Ruffalo previously denied pushing antisemitism in a statement to Fox News Digital after Paramount's original condemnation. "The accusation that I am antisemitic is appalling and fundamentally dishonest," Ruffalo said. "Criticizing the actions of the Israeli prime minister, a military technology contract or the executives who supply it is not the same as criticizing Jewish people." CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE The proposed transaction would place CNN, HBO and Warner Bros. studio assets under the Ellison family’s control. A coalition of 12 state attorneys general sued to block it on antitrust grounds, and the companies agreed not to close until five days after a court ruling on the merits or June 1, 2027, whichever comes first. Fox News Digital reached out to Ruffalo's representatives for additional comment. Fox News Digital’s Lindsay Kornick and CJ Womack contributed to this report.

CNN STAFFERS SEE PARAMOUNT MERGER AS 'INEVITABLE' DESPITE LEGAL BATTLE DELAYING ELLISON TAKEOVER Fonda knocked the proposed merger of Paramount Skydance and Warner Bros Discovery. articles.body:
McLaren and Ferrari had updates to check on Friday of the F1 Italian GP, as Mercedes practiced the tow, while Red Bull suffered from balance issues.

McLaren finally introduced its 'H-Wing' on Friday of F1 Italian GP at Monza , with good results. Lando Norris tried it in FP1, followed by both the Brit and Oscar Piastri using it in FP2. From the initial numbers, the team found it useful and mechanically working after earlier trials showed some gremlins.

McLaren, Ferrari scene after Friday in F1 Italian GP

They have been developing the part ever since it was spotted on Ferrari's car in pre-season testing. They are finally hopeful to use it for the full weekend after analysis on Friday evening. While the H-Wing worked, McLaren struggled a bit on the pace side when compared to its rivals.

Having found success in the last two events, Andrea Stella hopes that it can deliver in Monza, so that they can think of challenging their rivals. But they were a bit aloof of their immediate rivals, with Norris terming it as 'much trickier' than the last few Fridays they have had.

He feels they are lacking a bit everywhere and will have to work overnight to find that extra tenth to move up in the front row. Towards the end of FP2 session, McLaren ran a following simulation with both cars going back and forth for several laps, in preparation of race.

Over at Ferrari, the new power unit under ADUO seemed to have worked well on Friday. Neither Lewis Hamilton, nor Frederic Vasseur gave much about the extent but both were positive about delivery and performance. Although, they still think that they are down on the likes of Mercedes.

They had a good FP1 to be 1-2, but Hamilton dropped back in FP2 from Charles Leclerc. The Brit felt the changes he made didn't help him to extract the maximum and he might revert for FP3. Even though there is a scope of tow help in qualifying, Vasseur said they want two cars on the front row.

He thinks tow is a good idea in the case that the other car has a penalty, but for Ferrari, it is about putting two cars on the front row rather than one. That is the exact play at Mercedes, who practiced tow in FP1 , with Andrea Kimi Antonelli focusing on race pace for Sunday.

Despite no significant update, they found themselves to be in a good shape after George Russell set the pace in FP2. Team representative Bradley Lord hopes the bet put on by Fernando Alonso that Antonelli will be on the podium from the back, comes certainly true.

For Red Bull, it was balance issues again. After Max Verstappen missed FP1 for Ayumu Iwasa, he only had one session to get things aligned but it was a struggle. He finished only eighth, few hundreds ahead of Racing Bulls' Yuki Tsunoda. Aside balance, the Dutchman conceded that they are a bit behind overall.

"[It was] much trickier than the last few Fridays. We're struggling for pace quite a lot more than the last few. So, yeah, much trickier. We'll see what we can change overnight, but we're not in as good of a position compared to the last few weekends. So, yeah, tough. It's a bit everywhere, honestly. There's not one corner we're quicker than anyone else ahead of us. We lose a little bit in the straights comparing to Mercedes, which we kind of expect, but also the high speed is where we lose most of our lap time, which is normally where we're quick. So we have to try and figure out a few things, but we're just off the pace everywhere at the minute. [As for the following with Oscar was] just to see the following and the effectiveness."

"Well, you saw on the timesheets four-tenths off the quickest car, not where we ideally want to be. We feel like we've got a reasonable balance in the car at the moment. We played around with ride heights just to adjust performance between high and low speed. Reasonable there. From an energy perspective we've still got a bit of work to do. I think there's certainly lap time available to us. A little bit moving around recharge, moving around deployment. Drivers, maybe there's a tenth or so. And from the engineers, yeah, we'll extract a little bit from the setup. But realistically, I think it's going to be a challenge to be on pole, but we'll do what we can to get as close as possible tomorrow.

"Yeah, really, really pleased with the H-Wing. As you saw right from the start of the season, we've been developing. We brought it to an event previously, tested, and it's good to see it on the car. And from the sign-off that we've done at this event, mechanically, looks like we're fine to race it. And from an aero perspective, it does exactly as we expected it to. So no, really pleased to bring that extra performance to this event. Just shows we could have done with a little bit more, but yeah, I think everyone back at the factory, all the way through concept, design, manufacturing, and getting parts to the track for this event, brilliant job."

"The straight-line speed [the main limitation]. It's considerable, just looking at the deltas just there, I was losing something like six-tenths to George just in the straights, which is something we need to look into. And then just balance, it was really, really hard to pull the lap out of the car, was not an easy one to drive in FP2 for some reason. So we made a couple of changes, but shouldn't have really been bad. So we might revert, but we'll take a look and see if we can make it better for tomorrow.

"I think that's what we need to look into, if it's that, if it's deployment, but the engine is an improvement, which I'm really grateful for the guys back at the factory for working on. But our deployment schedule is different to the others, our competitors. But yeah, seems like they maybe have less drag for the straights, so it's something we need to definitely look at tomorrow. Yeah, the engine, it's really nice to drive with in the low speed. That's not been a problem, we've done a great job with that."

"No, but I think from session to session we are all using different levels of fuel, different engine modes and it's very difficult to read even for us. That means that we just have to be focused on ourselves and to try to get the best. We have a kind of convergence of the approach for FP3, but let's see. Still a long way until Sunday, looks like for the race pace you have different options in terms of energy deployment. For sure you will have opportunities. It's better if you are not on pole, but if you are on pole tomorrow, I would prefer a mega boring one.

"[For the power unit], yeah, but you have to keep in mind that performance in the straight line, it's the drag, it's the weight of the car, it's everything. It's not just the engine. And we did a step for sure, and we didn't bring aero too for nothing. I think we still have a decent gap. [And qualifying tow], no, that's why I think we have two cars. It's an advantage and I want to use the two cars. We have two cars on the first rows. Now that if we have one car starting from the back for sure you use it for the tow like Hadjar did for Max in Spa. It's a clever move, but I prefer to have two cars in front."

"It was a very different Friday compared to usual, focusing a lot more on the long run consecutive laps, but it was a good day. We got a lot of data and yeah, now looking forward to tomorrow. I think it's (overtake) going to be better than previous years because with energy you can do many different things, so it's going to be, you know, it's going to be very interesting. And today I did some running behind other cars to see the difference and yeah, it was very interesting to see the difference. [And yeah], we did try in FP1 some towing. I tried to give him a tow and just to take the reference for tomorrow and it looked to work quite well, so let's see tomorrow."

"Hey, if Fernando's bet (that Antonelli will be on podium from the back) pays off and it pays out for him, then we'll be very happy indeed. I mean, I think we're aiming to get up into solid points-paying positions. We saw George able to do that in Hungary after effectively starting from the back following the challenge he had off the start line. He was still able to get, back up there, so hard to put too precise a prediction on it just because you don't know how the race will unfold, what VSCs and safety cars might do.

"We've seen in the last few races we've been a little unlucky with VSCs, so maybe it's time for the wheels to turn on that one and something to play into our hands as well. [With tow,] I mean, we'll have a look at that and see what can make most sense in terms of how he can, you know, put a good lap in Q3, but also then work as a team to maximize George's chances as well. And I think they're both pretty clear that, just as we saw really good team cooperation in Zandvoort, then no reason to expect anything different this weekend in Monza."

"It was tricky to get the balance of the car right today and we will need to work on this for tomorrow to find a little bit more lap time. Our gap is still big compared to the front runners, but I hope that we can close it a little bit in Qualifying over one lap. Hopefully we will be even closer in the race and it will come together a bit more on the long runs, but this is trickier to predict. We are looking at what we can do overnight with the car and see if we can make some positive changes and try and get the true corner balance together. Of course, it was only FP2 for me today, but it was good that Ayumu got a chance to drive."

"I think clearly we have a balance issue on the car, main thing. A little bit like Zandvoort, to be honest, and try to understand what the issue is, try to fix it in a different way by setup and car components. But yeah, it's a main thing we are working on. What doesn't help is when Max is not driving during FP1 and you jump in the car there, that we have less time to react and now we have to react for FP3. It's a main thing.

"I think I'm never confident, otherwise we will never achieve anything. But it's what we are trying to do, and all the team are working hard to achieve it, yeah. It (deployment issue) should not be. You know, I think it's why the free practice is there, is to try to highlight the issue and try to after that fix it. But yeah, I think it's a normal weekend on that aspect. After, for Max, the main concern for me is the balance."
